summary.text: At \(n=140\), exact floor evaluations give \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\), using rational bounds on \(\sqrt5\). Hence the proposed right-hand side is \(528+484-471=541\), not \(a(161)=542\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor
\qquad(n\geq 1).
\]
Since \(\sqrt{5/4}=\sqrt5/2\), this may be written as
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor\frac{n\sqrt5}{2}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor.
\]
We disprove the proposed identity
\[
a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
by taking \(n=140\). Thus the four terms that must be evaluated are \(a(140),a(144),a(157)\), and \(a(161)\).

All the required floor evaluations can be established using exact integer comparisons. We use the elementary fact that for nonnegative real numbers, an inequality can be checked after squaring: if \(x,y\geq0\), then \(x\leq y\) if and only if \(x^2\leq y^2\), and similarly for strict inequalities. Since \(\sqrt5>0\), all quantities below are nonnegative.

First consider \(n=140\). We claim
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{140\sqrt5}{2}\right\rfloor
=\lfloor70\sqrt5\rfloor=156.
\]
Indeed,
\[
156^2=24336<24500=70^2\cdot5,
\]
so \(156<70\sqrt5\), while
\[
157^2=24649>24500=70^2\cdot5,
\]
so \(70\sqrt5<157\). Hence
\[
156<70\sqrt5<157,
\]
and therefore its floor is \(156\). Also \(\lfloor140/4\rfloor=35\). Consequently,
\[
a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471.
\]

Next consider \(n=144\). We claim
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{144\sqrt5}{2}\right\rfloor
=\lfloor72\sqrt5\rfloor=160.
\]
For the lower bound,
\[
160^2=25600<25920=72^2\cdot5,
\]
so \(160<72\sqrt5\). For the upper bound,
\[
161^2=25921>25920=72^2\cdot5,
\]
so \(72\sqrt5<161\). Thus
\[
160<72\sqrt5<161,
\]
which gives the asserted floor. Since \(\lfloor144/4\rfloor=36\), we obtain
\[
a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484.
\]

For \(n=157\), we claim
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{157\sqrt5}{2}\right\rfloor=175.
\]
The lower inequality \(175\leq157\sqrt5/2\) is equivalent, because both sides are nonnegative, to
\[
350\leq157\sqrt5.
\]
Squaring gives the exact comparison
\[
350^2=122500<123245=157^2\cdot5,
\]
so in fact \(350<157\sqrt5\), and hence \(175<157\sqrt5/2\). For the upper inequality, we compare with \(176\). We have
\[
352^2=123904>123245=157^2\cdot5,
\]
so \(157\sqrt5<352\), and therefore
\[
\frac{157\sqrt5}{2}<176.
\]
It follows that
\[
175<\frac{157\sqrt5}{2}<176,
\]
and the floor is \(175\). Furthermore, \(157=4\cdot39+1\), so
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{157}{4}\right\rfloor=39.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528.
\]

Finally consider \(n=161\). We claim
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{161\sqrt5}{2}\right\rfloor=180.
\]
For the lower endpoint, note that
\[
360^2=129600<129605=161^2\cdot5.
\]
Thus \(360<161\sqrt5\), so
\[
180<\frac{161\sqrt5}{2}.
\]
For the upper endpoint,
\[
362^2=131044>129605=161^2\cdot5.
\]
Thus \(161\sqrt5<362\), so
\[
\frac{161\sqrt5}{2}<181.
\]
Consequently,
\[
180<\frac{161\sqrt5}{2}<181,
\]
and its floor is \(180\). Also \(161=4\cdot40+1\), hence \(\lfloor161/4\rfloor=40\). Therefore
\[
a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\]

We now substitute these four exact values into the conjectured recurrence at \(n=140\). The conjecture would require
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
But the right-hand side is
\[
a(157)+a(144)-a(140)
=528+484-471
=1012-471
=541,
\]
whereas
\[
a(161)=542.
\]
Thus the asserted equation at \(n=140\) would say \(542=541\), which is false. Therefore the proposed recurrence does not hold for every \(n\geq1\), and the conjecture is disproved.
